📌 Data Leak Scams: Why Your Wallet Company Will Never Call You

Main Points
⏺ When a shop or service leaks customer data, scammers get your name, phone and address
⏺ They then call or write pretending to be "support" from your wallet brand
⏺ This post explains how these scams work and how to shut them down in one sentence



1️⃣ Core Idea — A leaked order list tells scammers exactly who owns a crypto wallet. That makes their fake "security alert" sound real. A reseller connected to Trezor recently reported a breach of roughly 27,000 orders.
2️⃣ Why It Happens — The leak doesn't touch your coins. It gives criminals your contact details, so the attack moves from your device to your trust.
3️⃣ Example — You get a call: "Your wallet was compromised, read us your recovery phrase so we can secure it." The caller knows your name and what you bought.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — Phone calls, SMS, emails with "urgent firmware updates", and even paper letters with a QR code to a fake site.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — No real wallet company will ever call you or ask for your seed phrase. Hang up, ignore the link, and only use the official app or website you type in yourself.
Final Thoughts

A data leak is a warning, not a theft. Your funds are safe as long as the seed phrase never leaves your hands — and nobody who asks for it is on your side.

🪙 THE NICKEL CALLED A FAKE THAT SOLD FOR $3.17 MILLION

Only five 1913 Liberty Head nickels are known. They were never part of the Mint's regular production, and collectors have chased them for more than a century.

North Carolina collector George O. Walton bought one in the mid-1940s for a reported $3,750. On March 9, 1962, he was killed in a car crash on his way to a coin show. The nickel was recovered from the crash site.

His heirs were told it was an altered-date fake. Walton's sister kept it in a closet in Salem, Virginia, for 41 years.

In 2003, her children answered a nationwide search for the missing fifth coin. At a convention in Baltimore, experts compared it with the other four in a secret midnight meeting and declared it genuine.

On April 25, 2013, Heritage Auctions sold it for $3,172,500.
